Howard Epps of Athens, while drnnk, Saturday, attempted to kill his sister with an ax.

At Brunswick Saturday twenty-two negroes paid $300 each for railroad fare to a negro who had engaged them to go to Florida to work on a railroad for $200 a day. They were to meet him at the depot that night to secure their tickets and start. They have not seen the contractor since.

Between McDonough and Tunis a few nights ago a negro entered a house occupied by a young lady named Dunn, and after dragging her out of doors committed a nameless crime against her person and left her unconscious on the ground. A negro named John Berry is under arrest. Miss Dunn says he is the guilty one.

An aged countryman went up to the court house at Athens Saturday and had a deed recorded which was issued in 1803. He said he heard the other day that he was not the owner of the property he claimed, although he had a deed to it, until the deed was recorded, and so brought it up to have things fixed. As a matter of fact his claim was all right, but finding out about "this recordin' business," nothing would suit him until he had it on record at the court house.

Saturday Queen Wells, a colored woman, a passenger on the Savannah, American and Montgomery train, was drowned at Oconee river bridge because of a misstep. She got off of the forward end of the coach to get on the rear end; walking back the length of the car, she attempted to board the train again, when she missed her footing and was precipitated into the river. The unfortunate woman was drowned before aid could reach her.

Old man Si Johnson, the old negro peanut vender, one of the landmarks of Albany, died Wednesday, having reached the age of 96 years. Old man Si served through the war of 1812 as the body servant of Col. John Gilmore, and served through the Mexican war in the same capacity with Col. John Gilmore, Jr. After that he became the property of Mack Johnson, with whom he went through the civil war. Old Si did not confine himself during those trying times to simply attending to the wants of his masters, but he shouldered his gun in a number of instances and fought with courage for the cause, in which they were engaged.

A special from Newnan to the Macon Telegraph says: "A terrible accident happened to W. H. Kersey, an employee of the Cole Manufacturing Company, while running a pattern lathe Friday afternoon. His chisel hung in the rim of the wheel and tore off a segment, which was thrown with terrific force and struck the unfortunate man in the eye. A pointed corner of the segment was forced into the socket of the right eye, destroying it beyond remedy, and also fractured the skull just above the eye. Drs. Peddy and Moore, who removed the eye-ball and fragments of bone, express the opinion that Mr. Kersey will recover, unless he received injuries which have not yet developed."

The law provides that when the tax return of any railroad is unsatisfactory, the property shall be assessed by a board of assessors, appointed by the governor and paid by the state. The compensation provided for it is $4 00 a day. The return of the Covington and Macon is unsatisfactory, being so reported by the controller general. The property, says the law, shall now be assessed. But it happens at the same time that there is not a single dollar in the treasury wherewith to pay the expense of assessment. To be one of the assessors is not only to work for nothing, but to pay one's own expenses as well. The board of assessors in the case of the Atlanta and Florida and the Savannah and Americus were out several days, paying their own expenses the while, and upon their return home paid a typewriter $5 to draw up their report in shape. They learned, upon presenting their accounts, that the last dollar of the contingent fund was gone, and that they had been working for nothing and paying their own expenses.

At Americus Saturday a little white girl was caught and whipped by a negro girl who was several years older than she. The child reported the occurrence to her mother. When the negro girl came up to the house the mother of the child called her to account about it. In answer to the lady, the negro girl offered her a direct insult. The lady gathered up a whip which was near by and administered a genteel whipping. The girl went home and told her parents of what had happened. About noon the negro girl's father appeared at the store of the white girl's father and commenced to curse and abuse him. The gentleman ordered the negro out of his store, but that worthy refused to go. He remained and added insult to insult until it was impossible for the gentleman to stand it any longer. At this juncture the gentleman took up an ax handle and let go at the negro's head. The blow was a telling one and the negro withdrew after he had received it. Four or five warrants were issued yesterday on account of this affair.

I. P. Sprake, a car inspector for the Savannah, Americus and Montgomery road, was run over and killed at Rocheile Saturday. Mr. Sprake was working on a car when an empty car struck it and ran over him. E. B. Carroll was under the car, and Mr. Sprake was standing between the car being worked on and another, holding a piece of timber. A car which was being loaded with naval stores, just above where the men were working, was turned loose and left to roll down the grade. The car went down rapidly and struck the one on which the men were working. Mr. Sprake was caught between the cars and his stomach crushed by the wheels. His back was badly mangled. Mr. Sprake only cried "Oh God!" and he was dead. Mr. Carroll had a narrow escape, only saving himself by clinging to the axle and letting it drag him along. He got out from under the car and gathered Mr. Sprake in his arms, in which position the unfortunate man died. All that saved Mr. Carroll was the fact that he was at the end of the car opposite the one struck by the runaway car.

The negro is charged with housebreaking and the case will be tried tomorrow. In the Trammell case the officer arrested George Bailey, colored, in O street last week, and the officer, it is charged, tapped him on the head with his club with such force that it was necessary for a physician to patch up Bailey's scalp with a needle and thread. Bailey was fined $5 in the Police Court and a charge against him of assaulting the officer and a charge against him. In this case a warrant for assault was issued against the officer and was subsequently nolle prossed by Mr. Armes.
Mr. Armes' action was complained of at last night's meeting and the three cases were referred to the next mass meeting of the association, which will be held Monday evening.

SAMPLE CASES SHOWING THE PIG-HEADEDNESS OF SOME POLICE OFFICERS. MEN ARRESTED ON TRIVIAL PRETEXTS. And in Many Instances Brutally Clubbed and Maltreated. A WEELING OUT IS VERY NECESSARY. Are They Merely Retaliating for the Way They Were Treated in the Army or Navy?
In connection with the article in THE CRITIC of Wednesday referring to the abuse of authority by members of the police force, and attendant evils which have grown out of it, is the large number of trivial arrests that have taken place recently, which were so apparently unjust and uncalled for that they were thrown out of court upon the hearing.

Among one of the most outrageous arrests and one for which the officer should be promptly disciplined, was that of Charles G. Leonard, assistant chief clerk of the Census, and Mr. Ernst of the population division. It was part of Mr. Leonard's duties to superintend the removal of schedules, and his presence was necessary on the sidewalk. Officer Loftus came along and ordered him to move on, and when he attempted to explain was arrested and taken to the station house, with his companion, on a charge of obstructing the sidewalk. When the matter was laid before Captain Austin he instantly ordered the men's release. Here was a case of

OFFICIOUS INTERFERENCE on the part of an officer with a Government official in the discharge of his duties, utterly uncalled for and unwarranted.

That ordinance relating to the obstruction of the sidewalks was never meant to apply to respectable citizens quietly conversing on matters of business on the sidewalk, and it is an assumption of authority on the part of an officer to attempt to make citizens "move on." Under such circumstances it is their right to refuse, and when in his offended indignation an officer arrests them he simply proves himself an unfit person to be a policeman. The law might apply to a disorderly gathering, and in that case it would be perfectly proper for the officer to arrest them. In deciding a similar case recently

THE COURT DISMISSED IT, and said that officers should exercise a great deal of discretion in making an arrest upon a charge of that kind.
Another flagrant abuse of power occurred a day or so previous to the arrest of Mr. Leonard, when Hon. John H. Smythe, ex Minister to Liberia, was arrested without provocation by Officer Trammell of the Second Precinct. The arrest was unnecessary, unprovoked and uncalled for. Mr Smythe had gone to the station-house to ascertain the facts in the arrest of a colored clampedlar, and, owing to a remark he made to the crowd, advising them not to follow the officer, was arrested himself in the station. He had a perfect right there, so the court decided, as did any other citizen who went to make proper inquiries, and the officer had no right to arrest him, because his feelings were hurt by the defendant's remarks, when he was

NOT VIOLATING ANY LAW.

Trammell has earned a reputation within the past year or so, for his extra officiousness, and it is such men as he he that have brought the force into disrepute.

On August 9, he had Arthur Talks in the Police Court on five separate charges, as follows: Profanity, playing baseball, breaking windows, throwing missiles (baseballs) and disorderly conduct. Any one of the charges would have covered the offense; but there was none, for Judge Mills promptly dismissed the cases against the young man.

Another outrageous case was the brutal clubbing of a respectable German, by the name of C. C. Sherman, at a picnic, on August 18, by Officer Cutler of the Ninth Precinct. It was shown on the trial of the case that the officer had been drinking and had committed

AN UNPROVOKED ASSAULT on the man, and then arrested him for protesting. His case is now before the trial board, and the chances are he will not much longer disgrace the uniform he wears.

A day or so ago a little colored boy who was watching the merry go round on Fourteenth street was ordered away, and when he did not move fast enough the officer arrested him for disorderly conduct. The case was dismissed.

But the crowning glory for the most asinine arrest on record must go to Officer Hanson. Day before yesterday he had arrested his next door neighbor, Mrs. Emma Sullivan, for disorderly conduct, and at the trial went on the stand and swore he made the arrest because her son whistled in the street in the morning and otherwise disturbed his rest. It was also developed that this officer agreed not to make the arrest if Mrs. Sullivan would.

GET DOWN ON HER KNEES before him, beg his pardon and chastise the boy, all of which she indignantly and properly refused to do. Such a man as that is a nice guardian of the peace—is he not? It may never have entered his colossal brain that if the noises disturbed him he could move.

On the night of September 1 another cutrage occurred at the Schuetzen Park, during which a one-legged man named Drake was brutally clubbed by Officer Hurd. There was a fight between two men, and Drake, who did not know either of them, attempted to separate them. When Officer Hurd came up the men ran away, but the gallant officer thought it his duty to make an arrest anyhow and grabbed Drake. The latter protested, but the officer brutally dragged him along and finally dealt him a heavy blow with his night stick. CONGRESSMAN QUINN. who was present, denounced the officer's action in the most vigorous language, as did a number of other well known gentlemen.

when he was at last satisfied that he had the wrong man, and said he was sorry he had clubbed him.

These are but a few of the many cases which have occurred recently. If it were necessary numerous others could be instanced, and yet all these officers are still wearing their badge of authority.

It is an undisputed fact that there are a large number of men on the force who are not qualified to hold the places they do. They come here from the Army or Navy and know nothing about Washington, its people or their surroundings. Only recently an officer was asked what river Washington was located on and he said Chesapeake Bay.

WHAT MAJOR MOORE SAYS.

"I have tried very hard," said Major Moore yesterday, "in making my selection of the thirty-two men this year, to pick out those whom I thought were qualified to hold the position. Men have come to me from the Marine Barracks or the Navy Yard with letters from their superior officers recommending them highly. I have paid but little attention to letters of that nature and have only accepted men on their own merits.

"It is a very hard matter," continued the Major, "to make comparisons as to the number of arrests. On July 30, 1886, the police force was composed of 267 men, and now we have 408, showing an increase of 141 new men. Of course we will have a continual increase in arrests, for out of the 141 additions made to the force 88 have been made this year and last."

As a whole the Major thought that they had a good many admirable officers, and only a very few indifferent ones.

In 1886 the department only had an appropriation of $344,780, whereas for this fiscal year the amount is $501,035.

"Could you give me any idea," asked the reporter, "as to how many efficient and how many inefficient officers you have on the force?"

"That would not be a proper question for me to answer," replied the Major. "We have a trial board to determine on these questions and you can readily see that I ought not to pass judgment on my men."

"It is a very hard matter anyhow to make any reliable comparison on the number of arrests made for it depends almost entirely on the condition of the weather. In the winter months when the people live indoors the percentage of arrests is very much smaller than in the summer months, when almost every one remains out in the air as much as possible.

VIRGINIA NEWS.
For the first time in several years the grape crop of Fauquier county has been a great success.

Miss Nettie Merchant, daughter of Cal. R. B Merchant, editor of the Fredericksburg Star, and Mr. Edgar Stearns, of Prince William county, were married in Fredericksburg yesterday.

Gov. McKinney has declined to interfere in the case of John Phillips, the negro under sentence to be hanged at Mecklenburg C H. on Friday for the murder of Captain R. C. Overby. Phillips, who is now in jail at Petersburg, will be taken to Mecklenburg today, under a military escort, to prevent his being lynched en route.

A rough-looking white man walked into a hardware store in Roanoke yesterday evening and asked for a revolver. One was shown to him, and at his request the clerk loaded it. Stepping back from the counter the stranger placed the weapon to his head and fired, the bullet entering the brain and causing instant death. A letter in the man's pocket was addressed to "W. C. Young, Roberta, Franklin county, Va." The man was under the influence of liquor.

On Tuesday in King George County Randolph Insoce, white and George Carter, a negro, got into an altercation, which resulted in a mortal wound to the negro. Insoce being closely pressed by Carter, drew a pistol and shot the negro. Insoce was arrested, brought before a magistrate, and bailed to appear at the next term of the County Court taken. It is said also that the trouble between the parties grew out of political talk and impudence on the part of the negro.

Celia Wormlev, colored, the oldest person in Shenandoah Valley, and perhaps the oldest person in the State, died at Middletown, July 30, aged 110 years. She was one of a large number of slaves owned by Conrad Carter, of Fauquier county, whose will provided that his slaves should all be free when 30 years of age. Hence "Aunt" Celia enjoyed eighty years of freedom. Four generations of her numerous descendents are represented there and elsewhere in the State. Her recollections of persons and events of the long time ago were clear and her vigor of mind and body remarkable. She was present at a prayer meeting of the colored people a short time before her death and joined heartily in the singing with a strong, clear voice.

A NEGRO MORTALLY WOUNDED
By a White Man in King George County
Political Insolence the Cause.
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]
[Special telegram to the Dispatch.]

FREDERICKSBURG, VA., August 13.—On yesterday in King George county Randolph Inscoe, a highly-respectable white man and George Carter, a negro, got into an altercation, which resulted in a mortal wound to the negro. Inscoe being closely pressed by the negro—and it is said in self-defence—drew a pistol and shot the negro. Inscoe was arrested, brought before a magistrate, and bailed to appear at the next term of the County Court of that county.

EXCITED.

It is said that much excitement prevails among both blacks and whites in the neighborhood of the difficulty, and serious trouble is apprehended in consequence. It is also rumored that the trouble between the parties grew out of political talk and impudence on the part of the negro, that being the Eighth congressional district, in which great excitement prevails as to the candidates for congressional honors.

KING GEORGE.
Shooting Affray in the County-Cause of the Difficulty. KING GEORGE C. H. VA. Aug. 14.
KING GEORGE C. H., VA., Aug. 14. [Special.]—About 12 o'clock yesterday Randolph Inscoe (white) and George Carter (colored) had an altercation near St. Paul's church, in this county, concerning some wood which they were hauling to the river, Carter asserting that Inscoe was putting wood in the road and thus shutting him (Carter) from the shore. In the quarrel Carter threw Inscoe down and inflicted two savage bites upon his face. Inscoe went to the house (home) and got his gun, and meeting Carter two hours afterwards, shot him in the thigh and abdomen, inflicting probably fatal wounds. At the preliminary examination before the magistrate last night there was much conflicting testimony concerning the shooting. All of the witnesses
george-carter-1890-08-12.A6: agreed that Carter was extremely abusive to Insoeo, and threatened his life. The magistrate (Justice Benjamin Weaver) bailed Insoeo in the sum of $100, conditioned for appearance at the next term of the County Court.

Rice.

The figures named in our market reviews are for the largest lots from first hands.

Domestic sorts are out, except a few straggling lots of high grades. Holders are quite indifferent about selling for prices that are actually below those of the South. Talmage said in a recent circular, "This is a phenomenal year in rice." Conditions are the reverse of those which ordinarily prevail, everything in favor of seller and no change likely for some time to come. Foreign sorts are active. Spot stocks are light, and all attractive styles find ready sale to arrive. Advices from abroad continue to note absence of good prime grades. We learn from a European correspondent: "Tendencies (in rice) are still upward, owing to a very brisk demand from all sides. Our mills, however, offer very sparingly, expecting to do much better in the further course of the season. Imports show a great falling off compared with former years. Stocks are melting away, and the quality of fresh arrivals turns out worse and worse. Latest reports from the East Indies show advancing prices of the raw material, owing to the rise in silver. By all this it will be seen that the position is very sound and strong."
